title: What are Compressed Oops, why are they enabled by default below a 32GB heap, and why can going from 31GB to 33GB heap actually increase memory usage?
shortTitle: What are Compressed Oops, and why can a 33GB heap use more memory than a 31GB heap?

s1_definition.profdef: Compressed Ordinary Object Pointers (Compressed Oops) are a JVM optimization on 64-bit platforms where object references are stored as 32-bit values instead of full 64-bit pointers. The JVM exploits the fact that objects are 8-byte aligned, so it can shift a 32-bit reference left by three bits to address up to 32 GB of heap. Below a roughly 32 GB heap the flag `-XX:+UseCompressedOops` is on by default; above that threshold the JVM silently disables it and reverts to full 64-bit references, which enlarges every reference field in every object.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh keeps a phone book where every contact's address is written in full: house number, street, city, pin code, country. That is a 64-bit pointer. Now imagine the bank gives every locker a number and the lockers are spaced exactly eight slots apart, so instead of writing a long address he just writes the short locker index and multiplies by eight to find the real spot. That short index is a Compressed Oop. It works beautifully as long as the building has at most a few billion lockers. The moment the vault grows past 32 GB the short index can no longer reach every locker, so the bank is forced to go back to writing the full long address everywhere, and suddenly every page of the phone book needs twice the space.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compressed Oops store references as 32-bit numbers shifted by three bits to reach 32 GB; cross that line and every reference doubles to 64 bits, so a bigger heap can actually hold fewer objects.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Compressed Ordinary Object Pointers (Compressed Oops) are a JVM optimization on 64-bit platforms where object references are stored as 32-bit values instead of full 64-bit pointers. The JVM exploits the fact that objects are 8-byte aligned, so it can shift a 32-bit reference left by three bits to address up to 32 GB of heap. Below a roughly 32 GB heap the flag `-XX:+UseCompressedOops` is on by default; above that threshold the JVM silently disables it and reverts to full 64-bit references, which enlarges every reference field in every object.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh keeps a phone book where every contact's address is written in full: house number, street, city, pin code, country. That is a 64-bit pointer. Now imagine the bank gives every locker a number and the lockers are spaced exactly eight slots apart, so instead of writing a long address he just writes the short locker index and multiplies by eight to find the real spot. That short index is a Compressed Oop. It works beautifully as long as the building has at most a few billion lockers. The moment the vault grows past 32 GB the short index can no longer reach every locker, so the bank is forced to go back to writing the full long address everywhere, and suddenly every page of the phone book needs twice the space.

**One line to remember:** Compressed Oops store references as 32-bit numbers shifted by three bits to reach 32 GB; cross that line and every reference doubles to 64 bits, so a bigger heap can actually hold fewer objects.

sections.s2_technical:
On a 64-bit JVM a raw object reference is naturally 64 bits, which is eight bytes. Most server applications allocate millions of objects, and most objects contain several reference fields pointing at other objects. If every one of those fields is eight bytes, the reference overhead alone can consume a large fraction of the heap. Compressed Oops attack this by observing that the JVM aligns every object on an 8-byte boundary, so the low three bits of any real heap address are always zero. Because those three bits carry no information, the JVM can drop them, store only a 32-bit value, and reconstruct the real 64-bit address at access time by shifting left by three. A 32-bit value addresses 2^32 slots, and each slot is 8 bytes apart, so the reachable range is 2^32 times 8, which is 32 GB. That is the origin of the magic number.

You can see and control this with flags. The relevant switch is `-XX:+UseCompressedOops`, and on a modern HotSpot JVM it is enabled automatically whenever the maximum heap you request with `-Xmx` is at or below the compressed-oops threshold. For example `java -Xmx30g -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep UseCompressedOops` will show the flag as `true`, whereas `java -Xmx40g -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep UseCompressedOops` will show it as `false`. You cannot force it on above the limit because the arithmetic simply cannot address the heap.

There is an intermediate trick called a shifted base or zero-based compressed oops. If the heap happens to start at address zero, the JVM only needs the shift and no addition. If the heap must start at a non-zero base, the JVM adds a base pointer after shifting, which costs one extra instruction per dereference. Around the 26 GB to 32 GB range the JVM may switch from zero-based to base-plus-shift mode, so even inside the compressed region very large heaps are slightly slower per reference.

The counterintuitive consequence is the real interview point. Suppose you have a service comfortably running at `-Xmx31g` with compressed oops. A capacity planner says "we have spare RAM, let us bump the heap to 33 GB for safety." The moment the heap crosses 32 GB, compressed oops turn off, every reference field in every live object grows from four bytes to eight bytes, and object headers grow too because the klass pointer inside the header is also a compressed reference. The effective capacity for application objects can drop so much that the 33 GB heap holds fewer business objects than the 31 GB heap did. This is why experienced engineers either stay safely under 32 GB or jump well past it, for example to 48 GB or more, so the extra raw capacity outweighs the per-reference penalty.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs an in-memory position cache that holds one lightweight object per open trade so the risk desk can revalue the book in milliseconds. During a market event the number of open positions exploded, and the operations team, seeing heap pressure, raised the maximum heap from 31 GB to 33 GB expecting more room. Instead the service started throwing out-of-memory errors sooner than before. This is exactly how Compressed Oops work: crossing the 32 GB boundary silently doubled the size of every reference field, so the larger heap actually held fewer position objects.

Problem 2 — The capacity team needs a way to measure, before touching production, how many bytes each cached object truly occupies under compressed versus uncompressed references, because the difference is invisible in the source code. This is exactly how object layout works: the number and width of reference fields, not the business logic, decides the footprint, and the JVM mode decides the width.

To make this concrete we will build a small runnable demo that models a position object with several reference fields, prints whether compressed oops are active by reading the JVM flag, estimates the per-object footprint under each mode, and shows how a cache sized for 31 GB overflows at 33 GB. The code will include a Position class with reference fields, a PositionCache that holds many positions, a HeapModeInspector that reports the active mode, and a FootprintEstimator that computes bytes per object under both modes. The demo main method will simulate loading positions until the modelled heap is exhausted and log how many fit in each mode.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run UNDER the 32GB line — compressed oops ON
java -Xmx31g -jar target/position-cache-service-1.0.0.jar

# Run OVER the 32GB line — compressed oops OFF
java -Xmx33g -jar target/position-cache-service-1.0.0.jar

# Confirm the flag the JVM actually chose
java -Xmx33g -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep UseCompressedOops
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a request to size the position cache for two candidate heaps, 31 GB and 33 GB, where each Position carries six reference fields.

Step 1: The HeapModeInspector reads the maximum heap from the running JVM. At 31 GB the maximum is at or below the 32 GB threshold, so it reports compressed oops are on and references are four bytes.

Step 2: The FootprintEstimator computes bytes per Position in compressed mode. The header is twelve bytes, six references at four bytes each is twenty-four bytes, giving thirty-six bytes, rounded up to forty bytes for 8-byte alignment.

Step 3: Dividing 31 GB by forty bytes gives the number of positions that fit under compressed oops. This is the large, happy number.

Step 4: Now the 33 GB heap is modelled. The inspector reports compressed oops off, so references become eight bytes and the header grows to sixteen bytes. Six references at eight bytes is forty-eight bytes, plus sixteen is sixty-four bytes, already aligned.

Step 5: Dividing 33 GB by sixty-four bytes gives the number of positions under uncompressed oops. Each object is sixty percent larger, so even with two extra gigabytes of heap, fewer positions fit.

Step 6: The demo compares the two counts, finds the 33 GB count is smaller, and logs a warning that crossing the boundary disabled compressed oops.

```
2026-10-30 17:45:01 INFO    JVM heap mode: Compressed Oops ON  (references = 4 bytes)
2026-10-30 17:45:01 INFO    31GB heap, compressed ON  -> 832045082 positions fit
2026-10-30 17:45:01 INFO    33GB heap, compressed OFF -> 553648128 positions fit
2026-10-30 17:45:01 WARNING Bigger 33GB heap holds FEWER positions than 31GB! Crossing 32GB disabled Compressed Oops.
2026-10-30 17:45:01 INFO    Cache now holds 1 position(s) for the risk desk.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Capacity request: size position cache for 31GB vs 33GB
    │
    ▼
  HeapModeInspector.compressedOopsEnabled()
    │ reads Runtime.maxMemory()
    ├─ 31GB  ≤ 32GB  → compressed ON  (ref = 4B, header = 12B)
    └─ 33GB  > 32GB  → compressed OFF (ref = 8B, header = 16B)
    ▼
  FootprintEstimator.bytesPerPosition()
    │ ON : 12 + 6×4 = 36 → align → 40 bytes
    │ OFF: 16 + 6×8 = 64 → align → 64 bytes
    ▼
  positionsThatFit(heap, mode)
    │ 31GB / 40B  = ~832M positions   (compressed)
    │ 33GB / 64B  = ~553M positions   (uncompressed)
    ▼
  Compare: 553M < 832M  →  WARNING
  Bigger heap, FEWER objects — boundary crossed
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Compressed Ordinary Object Pointers are a sixty-four-bit JVM optimization that stores object references as thirty-two-bit values instead of full eight-byte pointers. The JVM can do this because every object is aligned on an eight-byte boundary, so the lowest three bits of any real address are always zero and carry no information. It drops those three bits, keeps a thirty-two-bit value, and reconstructs the real address at access time by shifting left by three. A thirty-two-bit value times the eight-byte alignment reaches exactly thirty-two gigabytes, which is why the feature is enabled by default only below a thirty-two gigabyte heap and is turned off automatically above it.

The reason it matters so much is that server applications hold millions of objects, and most objects contain several reference fields pointing to other objects. Halving the width of every reference from eight bytes to four bytes, and shrinking the class pointer inside each object header, can save a very large fraction of the heap. So compressed oops are not a micro-optimization, they are often the difference between a service fitting in memory and not.

The counterintuitive part, and the reason this is a favourite interview question, is what happens when you cross the thirty-two gigabyte line. In a project at National Bank of India we ran an in-memory risk position cache sized comfortably at a thirty-one gigabyte heap. During a volatile session the team raised the heap to thirty-three gigabytes expecting more capacity, and the service began failing with out-of-memory errors sooner than before. The cause was that crossing thirty-two gigabytes silently disabled compressed oops, every reference field in every position object doubled from four to eight bytes, the headers grew too, and the bigger heap actually held fewer business objects than the smaller one.

The practical lesson I carry from that is to treat thirty-two gigabytes as a cliff, not a smooth ramp. Either you stay safely under it, for example at thirty or thirty-one gigabytes, and keep compressed oops, or if you genuinely need more you jump well past it, to forty-eight gigabytes or more, so the extra raw capacity clearly outweighs the sixty percent per-object penalty. The dead zone between thirty-two and roughly forty gigabytes is the worst place to be, because you pay for uncompressed references without enough extra heap to make up for it. I verify the actual decision the JVM made by reading the UseCompressedOops flag with PrintFlagsFinal rather than assuming, because the switch is automatic and invisible in the application code.
